name: ScatterChart
intent: Two measures against each other, one dot per record, so a pattern between them shows: spend against usage, days late against balance.
usage: Use ScatterChart to look for a relationship between two numbers across many records. It is one component: pass series, each with its points of x and y. A point can carry a third measure as size, which draws it as a bigger dot by area, so twice the value looks about twice as big. Give each point a label and the tooltip names the record. xName and yName are written by their axes, since a scatter says nothing without them. Hover anywhere near a dot and the nearest one answers; the arrow keys walk the dots in the order they were given. See contracts/scatterchart.json for the full contract. Inside a loading page it draws its own skeleton in place: the page says loading once (FormLayoutContext, which RecordPage, ListPage, FormPage and Dashboard set), and it takes no loading prop of its own. The title stands as a bar at the length its words will take and the drawing as a faintly framed box of bars at the chart's own height (BP COBALT "chart skeleton"), so the chart arrives where its bars stood.

label.note: Names the chart for screen readers and captions its data table, like Spend against usage by account.

title.note: Visible title over the chart. The screen-reader name still comes from label.

subtitle.note: A quieter line under the title, like 120 accounts, last 30 days.

showHeader.note: Turns the title and subtitle off when the Card or Section around the chart already says the same.

series.itemShape: { name: string; intent?: ChartIntent; points: { x: number; y: number; size?: number; label?: string }[] }
series.note: One entry per group of dots, like a plan tier or a region. intent picks the colour; by default series take the kit's series order, pink, orange, gray, cyan, mint, green, olive, yellow and purple. size on a point draws it bigger, by area, against the largest size in the chart.

xName.note: The name of the measure along the bottom, written under the axis. A scatter without it says nothing.

yName.note: The name of the measure up the start, written beside the axis.

xFormat.note: How the x values read. Axis ticks are short; the tooltip and table show the full number.

yFormat.note: How the y values read, which is often not the same as x.

currency.note: The currency code for either format set to currency.

showGrid.note: Faint lines across the chart at the y ticks.

showLegend.note: The keys under the chart. Turn it off for a single series the title already names.

animate.note: Fades the dots in on first paint, a series at a time. Never plays when the person prefers reduced motion.

height.note: Height of the drawing in px, axis labels included. The width fills the container.

emptyLabel.note: What the chart says in place of the drawing when there are no points.

useWhen: Looking for a relationship between two measures across many records, like spend against usage by account.
Finding the records that sit apart from the rest, like a high balance that is also very late.
Comparing groups of records on the same two measures: one series per group.
A third measure that only needs to read as bigger or smaller: size on the point.
doNot: Do not use it for a trend over time. Time belongs on an ordered axis: use LineChart.
Do not use it for a handful of records. Three dots are a Table; a scatter earns its place past a few dozen.
Do not use it for categories. Use BarChart.
Do not leave xName and yName out. Two unnamed axes cannot be read.
Do not use size for a measure people must read off the chart. It says bigger or smaller, not how much.
Do not draw charts with loose SVG or a chart library. Use the kit charts.
Do not use raw hex; pick an intent.
a11y: A figure named by label. The drawing is hidden from screen readers; a visually hidden table holds every dot, named by its point label or its series and number, with its x, y and size.
The chart takes focus: the arrow keys walk the dots in the order they were given (Home and End jump to the ends) and show the same tooltip as pointing at them. Escape hides it.
The picked dot takes the kit's selection outline, so the pick does not rest on colour.
Series come with a legend and the tooltip names the record and both measures, so colour is not the only way to tell them apart.
Motion is subtle and optional (animate), and never plays when the person prefers reduced motion.
snippet:
<ScatterChart
  label="Spend against usage by account"
  xName="Credits used"
  yName="Monthly spend"
  yFormat="currency"
  series={[{ name: "Enterprise", points: [{ x: 1200, y: 4800, label: "Northwind Traders" }] }]}
/>
